title: Greek Dark Ages
capsule: The Greek Dark Ages (c. 1100–800 BCE) designate the period of societal collapse following the destruction or abandonment of Mycenaean palace centres around 1180–1150 BCE. The collapse entailed the disappearance of Linear B literacy, the dissolution of long-distance trade networks, a sharp decline in monumental construction, and a population contraction of perhaps 50–75 percent in some regions. The causes remain debated — drought, internal conflict, disruptions associated with the Sea Peoples, and systems collapse have all been proposed — and the severity varied regionally, with Attica and Euboea showing greater continuity. Recovery accelerated after 900 BCE with the adoption of the Phoenician alphabet (c. 800 BCE), renewed Mediterranean trade, and the social differentiation that prepared the ground for the Archaic polis.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Greek Dark Ages is a historiographical concept rather than a polity with borders; its geographic coverage across the Aegean is reconstructed from settlement survey data and is inherently approximate.
